newsitem.title: UK: Peptide links with SmithKline on allergy jabs.
newsitem.headline: Peptide links with SmithKline on allergy jabs.

text.p: Peptide Therapeutics Ltd has formed a strategic alliance with SmithKline Beecham plc (SB) to develop and market Peptide's allergy vaccine portfolio, Britain's BTG Plc said on Monday.

The allergy vaccine, originally licensed from BTG, has the potential to protect against a wide range of allergies such as hayfever and food allergies, irrespective of the agent causing the allergy, BTG said.

In 1994, BTG licensed the vaccine technology to Peptide for human applications and assigned certain technologies in return for equity and other considerations. In 1996, BTG licensed Peptide to develop veterinary applications for the vaccine.
To facilitate the alliance with SB, BTG and Peptide have replaced existing agreements between them with new arrangements such as BTG assigning the allergy vaccine patents to Peptide.
BTG's holding in Peptide following the SB deal will be marginally diluted to 4.5 percent from 4.8 percent, but BTG will continue to receive certain other payments based on the success of the company.

These vaccines address growing markets currently worth in more than 5.0 billion stg per year. Under the terms of the agreement with SB, Peptide could receive in excess of 30 million stg in licence and milestone payments, as well as substantial royalties on products sales.
The alliance will continue the research and development of the allergy vaccine portfolio, the lead product of which has successfully completed a Phase II clinical trial.
SB has also acquired exclusive worldwide rights to market products arising from the alliance.
The allergy vaccine technology has the potential to protect against all allergies in which the antibody IgE acts to mediate the allergic response.
These include major allergic conditions such as hayfever, juvenile asthma, anaphylaxis and food allergy in humans, and flea allergic dermatitis in dogs.

The original technology was developed by Professor Denis Stanworth and his team at the Rheumatology and Allergy Research Unit (RARU), University of Birmingham. BTG funded work over a number of years and filed critical patents covering the technology worldwide.
